title: Binomials
subtitle: odds and ends, give and take, sooner or later
summary: Use fixed pairs of words joined by and or or - peace and quiet, back and forth, sink or swim - in the correct, unchangeable order.

lesson.heading: What are binomials?
lesson.text: Binomials are expressions, often idiomatic, where two words are joined by a conjunction - usually *and*. The order is fixed: you cannot reverse it.

examples.text: Let's get the main things packed - we can do the **odds and ends** later.
examples.note: odds and ends = small, unimportant things

examples.text: Every relationship needs a bit of **give and take** to be successful.

lesson.note: You can often recognise a binomial by its sound: the two words start with the same sound or they rhyme.

lesson.heading: Binomials with a sound pattern
rows: an important part of something; belonging to it
a state of decay or ruin
of a poor standard or quality
entertain someone, take them out to restaurants
in a very difficult situation, with no help
lesson.note: Tears are **part and parcel** of growing up. The old cottage has gone to **rack and ruin**.

lesson.heading: Pairs of near synonyms
lesson.text: In many binomials the two words mean almost the same thing. The pair is simply stronger or more idiomatic than either word alone.

examples.text: You can **pick and choose** - it's up to you.
My English is progressing **in leaps and bounds**.
It's nice to have some **peace and quiet** now that the children have left.
The doctor recommended some **rest and recreation**.
examples.note: = relaxation; often shortened to R and R

examples.text: **First and foremost**, you must work hard.

lesson.heading: Binomials made of grammar words
rows: There are cafes **here and there** along the sea front.
on and off / off and on
back and forth / to and fro
I've been running **back and forth** all day.
going out again after an illness
She's better now, and **out and about** again.
She ran **up and down** the street.

lesson.heading: Binomials linked by other words
lesson.text: Not every binomial uses *and*. Several common ones are joined by **or**, **to** or **but** - and the order is just as fixed.

examples.text: You've got your sweater on **back to front**.
He won't help her - she'll have to **sink or swim**.
examples.note: = survive or fail on her own

examples.text: **Slowly but surely**, I realised the boat was sinking.
**Sooner or later**, you'll learn your lesson.
It's about the same distance as from here to Dublin, **give or take** a few miles.

lesson.heading: Two more with or
lesson.text: **All or nothing** means there is no middle way, and **take it or leave it** means this is the only offer, so accept it or don't.

examples.text: She didn't want to be just friends - it had to be **all or nothing**.
Well, I'm sorry, that's all I can offer you - **take it or leave it**.

lesson.text: Three very neutral binomials you will hear every day: an old **black and white** photograph; **Ladies and gentlemen**, your attention please; she ran **back and forth**. Never reverse them.

exercises.prompt: Match the first half of each binomial with its second half.
The receptionist is always so terribly ___; the whole atmosphere seems very formal.
exercises.explanation: Prim and proper = rather formal and fussy.

exercises.prompt: They stole my wallet, so I was left ___, with no one to help me.
exercises.explanation: To be left high and dry is to be left in a very difficult situation.

exercises.prompt: The room's a bit ___ but you're welcome to stay as long as you like.
exercises.explanation: Rough and ready = of a poor standard or quality.

exercises.prompt: That old house in the country has gone to ___; nobody looks after it now.
exercises.explanation: To go to rack and ruin is to fall into decay.

exercises.prompt: She was in a bad temper and was ___ at everybody.
exercises.explanation: Rant and rave = shout angrily. The order is fixed: rant comes first.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite in bold: 'Most importantly of all, I want to get a good, steady job.'
exercises.explanation: First and foremost = first and most importantly.

exercises.prompt: Her violin playing seems to be progressing ___.
exercises.explanation: To progress in leaps and bounds is to improve very fast.

exercises.prompt: I've bumped into Karen ___ but I don't meet her regularly.
exercises.explanation: On and off (or off and on) = occasionally.

exercises.prompt: We'll have to stay in a cheap hotel. We can't afford to ___.
exercises.explanation: To pick and choose is to have a wide choice and take only what you want.

exercises.prompt: Mrs James was ill for a while, but now she's ___ again.
exercises.hint: (three words - going out and doing things)
exercises.explanation: To be out and about is to be going out again after an illness.

exercises.statement: I love those old white and black Hollywood films from the 1940s.
exercises.explanation: The fixed order is black and white: I love those old black and white Hollywood films.

exercises.statement: Later or sooner you will learn that he is not a true friend of yours.
exercises.explanation: The binomial is sooner or later: Sooner or later you will learn that he is not a true friend of yours.

exercises.statement: Slowly but surely my English got better and soon I felt fairly fluent.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Slowly but surely = gradually, and the order is fixed.

exercises.prompt: Which word joins the two halves of each binomial?
Put the words in order. Robin's office is on the next floor to mine, so ...
exercises.answer: we have to go up and down all day
exercises.explanation: Up and down = in both directions.
